title: John Knox
hook: a firebrand preacher shapes the Church of Scotland and its schools

segments.voice: Yesterday, cognitio: knowing God and knowing ourselves. Your line was two knowledges.

A man chained to an oar. He's Scottish, a priest turned Protestant preacher, captured when the castle where he was preaching fell to a French force. Now he rows a French galley as a prisoner, pulling the same heavy oar day after day, not knowing if he'll ever see Scotland again. He does. Years later he comes home and preaches so fiercely that crowds pour out of the church and into the streets. His name is John Knox, and he left Scotland a church and an idea about schools that outlasted his anger.
screen: `A CHURCH, AND AN IDEA ABOUT SCHOOLS.`

segments.voice: Knox was a firebrand, and there's no softening it. After the galleys he spent time in exile, including in Calvin's Geneva, and came home convinced the church needed rebuilding from the ground. His preaching stirred crowds, and some tore apart altars and images in the churches. He wrote a furious pamphlet against women rulers. He argued face to face with Mary, Queen of Scots, a Catholic queen, and the meetings are remembered as storms. For Scotland's Catholics, the change he led meant losing their Mass and their churches, and that loss is part of the story too. But one piece is quieter. When Knox and his fellow ministers set out a plan for the new church, the First Book of Discipline, they wrote about schools: a schoolmaster in every parish, so children could learn to read, the poor as well as the rich, with colleges in the larger towns and universities above them. Part of the reason was simple: if every Christian should read the Bible, every child needs to read. That's an old idea in a new place. In the King James Bible, Moses tells the people to teach God's words "diligently unto thy children" and to talk of them "when thou sittest in thine house." Knox's plan put that at the scale of a country. It wasn't all built at once, and the money was fought over. But the idea took root. The Church of Scotland grew from this time, and after Knox it settled into a Presbyterian church, run by elders rather than bishops. So did the picture of a schoolhouse beside every church.

Remember who taught you to read: a parent with a picture book, a first-grade teacher, a librarian, and hold that person in mind. Then think of someone still learning, a child, a new reader, someone learning a new language, and one small way you could help. If you pray, give thanks for your teachers; if you don't, simply remember them with gratitude.
John Knox. A fierce Scottish preacher who helped shape the Church of Scotland, and whose plan called for a school in every parish.
Your line: a school in every parish. Rich and poor alike, learning to read. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: The Church of Scotland and Presbyterian churches elsewhere trace their roots to the Scottish Reformation, in which Knox was a leading voice; they are governed by elders, and look back to the First Book of Discipline's plan for parish schools.
